# PART 4 – The published model {#part-4-the-published-model .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 4
:::

::: notes
The last part fits the model of the original author to the respondents. Its structure is the multilevel structure of Part 2, with the characteristics of the respondents and the two national rates added, and the question is how it relates to the two-way design of the panel used by the reproduced specification, to which the answer depends on the years.
:::

## The published model {#the-published-model .smaller}

::: {.small}
- "citizens (Level 1; N: 390,373) are sampled within 16 EB waves (Level 2) that repeatedly took place within the 27 EU countries (Level 3)" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]
- The score of each respondent on sex, age, education, occupation and the type of community, with the national rates of growth and unemployment, and random intercepts for countries and for the country-waves of the surveys
- Model 1 of the paper adds interactions of the two rates with education, so its unemployment coefficient, −0.00340 in Table 3, is the slope of the lowest education band
- On the rebuilt respondents the workshop's refit gives `r fmt_num(oa_published$b, 5)` for the lowest band (t = `r fmt_num(oa_published$t, 2)` on `r fmt_num(oa_published$df_satterthwaite, 1)` Satterthwaite df), and without the interactions `r fmt_num(oa_no_interactions$b, 5)` (t = `r fmt_num(oa_no_interactions$t, 2)` on `r fmt_num(oa_no_interactions$df_satterthwaite, 1)` df), the mark "OA design" of the class chart at r = `r fmt_num(oa_no_interactions$r_on_df, 3)`
:::

::: {.src}
companion/multilevel.qmd, section 5; companion/_model-outputs/reference_refits.csv.
:::

::: notes
The original author describes the structure in one sentence, citizens sampled within sixteen waves within twenty-seven countries. The model regresses the framing score of each respondent on sex, age, education, occupation and the type of community, with the national rates of growth and unemployment and random intercepts for the countries and for the waves of the surveys. Model 1 of the paper also interacts the two rates with education, so its printed unemployment coefficient is the slope of the lowest education band. The workshop refitted the design on the rebuilt respondents both ways, and the refit without the interactions, whose slope averages over the bands, is the mark labelled OA design on the class chart. Both refits leave out the respondents who named nothing, as the code of the original author did, which is why that slope is steeper than the one in Part 3, where those respondents score zero.
:::

## Two designs {#two-designs .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: d3-designs-table
# The unemployment coefficient, with t, under the two-way design of the panel
# (growth adjusted for, conventional t) and under the published design without
# its interactions on the real respondents (Satterthwaite t), with and without
# terms for the years (companion/_model-outputs/person_year_effects.csv)
designs |>
  datawizard::data_modify(value = paste0(fmt_num(estimate, 5), " (", fmt_num(t, 2), ")")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("design", "outcome", "value")) |>
  datawizard::data_to_wide(id_cols = "design", names_from = "outcome", values_from = "value") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    Design = unname(c(two_way = "Two-way fixed effects, the panel",
                      published = "Published design, the respondents",
                      year_random = "Published, with random intercepts for years",
                      year_dummy = "Published, with a dummy for each year")[design])
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("Design", Cosmopolitan = "cosmo", Libertarian = "lib")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:3, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.75)
```

::: {.small}
- The published design has no year effects, model D in the typology of @Schmidt-CatranFairbrother2016RandomEffectsMultilevel, so a shock that hit every country at once, such as 2009, stays in its estimate. Their advice is "to include random effects at all potentially relevant levels" (p. 23)
- A term for the years brings the published estimate close to the slope of the panel, and on the libertarian scale it removes the association altogether
:::

::: {.src}
companion/multilevel.qmd, section 7; companion/_model-outputs/person_year_effects.csv, fitted with the country-years in place of the country-waves of the paper.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
When an effect appears under one defensible design and not under another, the design belongs in the preregistration, fixed before any model is fitted.
:::

::: notes
Here the country-year panel and the model of the original author disagree, and the reason lies in the years. The published design has random intercepts for countries and for the waves within them but nothing for the years, so nothing in it removes a shock that hit every country at once, as 2009 did. The fits in the table use the country-years as the middle level in place of the waves, so the row of the published design differs a little from the slope of Part 3. With a random intercept or a dummy for each year, the published estimate comes close to the two-way slope of the panel, and on the libertarian scale a term for the years removes the clear positive association that the published design finds. [advance] A result that appears under one defensible design and vanishes under another is, I think, a strong reason for fixing the design before any model is fitted.
:::

## The reading and the next session {#the-reading-and-the-next-session .smaller}

::: {.small .nonincremental}
- **The reading**: [Multilevel models](../companion/multilevel.html), the module of the companion curriculum behind this session, with the saved output of every model fitted to the respondents and the code that fits each model on your own file, sections on weights, bounded outcomes and the education gap of the second hypothesis, and a task that takes the within–between split to the respondents. For learning the models from the start: [Multilevel models](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-immigration/companion/multilevel.html) on the site of the Immigration and trust case study, @SnijdersBosker2012MultilevelAnalysisIntroduction and @GelmanHill2007DataAnalysisUsing
- **Next**: Bayesian estimation. The slope of the claim on the panel as a posterior distribution: priors and what they imply, partial pooling across countries, the uncertainty of a result with few clusters, and the checks that a Bayesian workflow runs before a posterior is read
:::

::: notes
The module Multilevel models is the reading for this session. It shows the saved output of every model fitted to the respondents, with the code that fits each model on your own file, and adds what this session could only mention, survey weights, bounded outcomes and the education gap of the second hypothesis of the paper, which only the respondents can test, and its task takes the within–between split of this morning to the respondents, as Fairbrother proposes. Snijders and Bosker, and Gelman and Hill, are the textbooks from which to learn the models. The next session returns to the panel and states the slope of the claim as a posterior distribution, where partial pooling across countries comes back from the Bayesian side, and so does the problem of few clusters.
:::
